title: Errors, audit logs and metrics
idea: Good error handling throws typed domain errors with stable codes, logs each business event once in a structured form, and counts outcomes so you can monitor them.
points: Domain errors extend one base class and carry a stable `code` field.
Only the edge, such as an HTTP handler, maps codes to status codes.
`AuditLogger` writes one structured line per business event through an injected sink.
Counters for created and rejected bookings feed dashboards and alerts.

steps.caption: A request to book `r2` at 9:30 reaches the handler, which calls `service.book()`.
The service loads the room's bookings and asks the policy about the slot.
The slot overlaps a 9 to 10 booking. The policy answers true, so `save` is never called.
The service counts the conflict, and `AuditLogger` records `booking.rejected` with the reason.
Then the service throws `RoomTakenError` with code `ROOM_TAKEN`.
The handler maps `ROOM_TAKEN` to 409. An unknown error becomes 500 with no internal details.

code.title: Typed domain errors
code.caption: Callers branch on `code` and `instanceof`, never on message text. Add a `RoomNotFoundError` mapped to 404.

walk.text: One base class sets `name` from `new.target`, so each subclass names itself.
Each failure the requirements allow gets its own class and stable code.
The edge maps codes to HTTP status; anything unexpected becomes a plain 500.
Two domain errors, one programming bug, and the name the base class set.

code.title: Audit log and counters
code.caption: The sink is injected, so a test can collect lines in an array. Replace `console.log` on line 28 with `() => {}`: the audit lines vanish, but the counts still print.

walk.text: `AuditLogger` turns an event and its fields into one JSON line for its sink.
`Metrics` counts named outcomes; a monitoring system would read the snapshot.
On a conflict: count it, log it once with a reason, then throw.
On success: save, count and log the business event.
Two bookings succeed and one is rejected; the caller sees only the code.

pitfalls: Never leave an empty `catch`; handle the error or let it travel up.
Log an error once, where it is handled, not at every layer it passes.
Keep personal data and tokens out of audit lines; log ids instead.

quiz.why: Subclassing keeps `instanceof` working, but `name` is inherited from `Error.prototype` unless a constructor sets it.

takeaway: Throw typed errors, log each event once, and count every outcome.
